prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate economic shocks, generating credit cycles
for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory and the analysis of the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a clean, original two-author mechanism. Collateral values and borrowing limits feed back on each other and turn small shocks into persistent, amplified cycles. It is the conceptual base of macro-financial modelling and of post-2008 thinking on financial stability, and it has about three decades of extension, quantitative use and policy application. It has the least attribution ambiguity among the candidates I rank highly. Melitz (2003) changed how trade is modelled. Selection into exporting and reallocation across firms became a new channel for gains from trade, and trade analysis moved to firm-level micro data. More than twenty years of empirical and structural work confirm it. Trade has not been recognised since 2008, and the work is a distinct later advance rather than a restatement of new trade theory. I cannot name Helpman here because the configuration is capped at three people, and I treat that as a cost of the cap rather than a verdict on his claim. My own method is to test theory against hand-collected real contracts and data. Both parts fit that standard: a sharp mechanism on one side, and a framework tied closely to firm-level evidence on the other.
statement.case_against: Both parts have attribution weaknesses. Melitz alone omits Helpman, whose joint work with Melitz and Yeaple (2004) on exporting versus FDI and whose broader trade agenda are substantial. It also leaves out the parallel empirical and quantitative work of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, who are not on the ballot entry. Kiyotaki-Moore sits next to the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator, and Bernanke's 2022 prize arguably overlaps in theme. The empirical identification of collateral channels is also less clean than the theory. A two-part prize that combines macro-finance with trade, with one part credited to a single person, may look like a construction forced by the cap rather than a natural pairing.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B007 first with Kiyotaki and Moore as the natural pair. He argues that the financial-accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist) overlaps with Bernanke's 2022 prize, so those two names should not be added.
responses.response: This persuades me to revise my opening, which included Gertler. Gertler's contribution is the accelerator with Bernanke and the later intermediary-frictions work. That is a separable discovery, and the 2022 recognition makes its marginal case weaker. The two-author collateral mechanism is the more defensible attribution, so I now propose only Kiyotaki and Moore. I would still want Gertler's work discussed explicitly as a possible separate strand rather than silently dropped.

responses.point: Krusell also ranks B007 first. He proposes adding Gertler as a third name because his work extends the mechanism into a quantitative financial-frictions and intermediary literature.
responses.response: I agree that Gertler's later work developed the quantitative literature, and I proposed him myself in the opening. The difficulty is that his credit overlaps with the Bernanke-linked accelerator and also competes with his place on B012. A narrower prize also leaves a name free under the three-person cap. I would revisit the question if the Committee frames the discovery broadly as financial frictions rather than as the collateral-amplification mechanism.

responses.point: Dreber ranks law and finance (B001) first for its broad and durable influence. She flags that the causal interpretation of legal origin has been challenged and that some measures, such as the anti-director index, were later revised.
responses.response: Her robustness concern is the main reason I have moved B001 from my second-ranked position to an alternative rather than a preferred part. The programme is influential and I would support it in a different configuration. However, measurement revisions, endogeneity critiques and the four-way authorship against a three-name cap leave a weaker foundation than a mechanism with a clean theoretical statement. My corporate-finance background makes me more sympathetic to the topic, which is another reason I do not want to lean on it.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first. She sees Melitz (2003) as the central contribution and Helpman as the natural second laureate through Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple. She regards Redding's work as more derivative of the original framework.
responses.response: I agree that Melitz is the clearest originator, and that is the basis for naming him alone. Her case for Helpman is strong, and I would prefer to include him. Under my configuration he cannot be added without removing a name from B007. If the Committee chooses B026 as a single-part prize, I would support Melitz and Helpman together. I would not credit Redding at this stage, though I take her point that his quantitative extensions are real.

responses.point: Andersson ranks the New Keynesian framework (B012) first with Taylor, Woodford and Gali. He acknowledges that excluding Calvo, Christiano and Eichenbaum leaves important contributors out and that credit is diffuse.
responses.response: I agree with his own qualification. The policy influence of the framework is very large and I do not dispute its Nobel-level importance. With eight credited names spread across the pricing model, the policy rule, the synthesis and the estimated DSGE work, a three-person cut is hard to defend on attribution grounds. This is why I keep B012 as an alternative rather than a preferred part. I would reconsider if the Committee settles the lineage question first, for example by deciding which strand is the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether a Melitz-only part is acceptable when Helpman's joint work with Melitz and Yeaple is substantial, and whether the three-person cap should instead push the Committee to a different pairing.
Whether Gertler's financial-accelerator and intermediary-frictions work should be credited alongside Kiyotaki-Moore, given the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig.
How far Melitz's credit should be separated from Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, who are not on the ballot entry, and from Krugman's 2008 prize.
Whether the Committee wants a two-part prize at all, given that opening support for B026 and B007 is spread across different member groups.
I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or the empirical record beyond the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of my listed co-authors appear among the credited names of B007 or B026. I note only that my corporate-finance field is close to the law-and-finance alternative (B001), and that I hold an adjunct position at Chicago Booth. Neither is a personal connection that requires recusal, and I disclose them without adjudicating.
